title: AI in HR: Which Tasks Can AI Support and Which Stay With a Person
summary: Small businesses can use AI in HR to answer routine questions and move paperwork faster while people stay in charge of the moments employees care about most. This article draws on TriNet’s 2027 State of the Workplace report to show which HR tasks employees and employers want AI to handle, which they want kept with a person, and why. You’ll leave with a task-by-task guide and six steps for introducing AI in HR with a clear route to a person.
body_markdown:
AI is part of the working week at most small and midsize businesses now, and HR teams are now figuring out which tasks an AI assistant can support and what to keep with a human. AI in HR can best when considered task by task, with AI supporting routine questions and paperwork and people handling moments that involve judgment, pay, health, or conflict.


TriNet's[2027 State of the Workplace report](https://www.trinet.com/resources/research/state-of-work) surveyed employers and employees at companies with 5 to 500 employees to see which HR tasks each side wants AI to support and which they want kept with a person. This article covers what AI in HR is, how small businesses use it today, a task-by-task guide for deciding where AI can provide support, and six steps to help get started.


## What is AI in HR?


**AI in HR** is the use of artificial intelligence tools to answer employee questions, support routine HR paperwork, draft documents, and surface patterns in workforce data, while HR professionals make the decisions.


Small and midsize businesses use four types of AI in HR:


- **AI assistant or HR chatbot** : Answers pay, PTO, and benefits questions inside the HR platform. An employee asks, "How much PTO do I have left?" and gets an answer mere moments.
- **Generative AI** : Drafts job descriptions, policy summaries, and review templates. A manager starts a performance review and AI suggests language based on the employee's role and recent feedback.
- **Workflow automation** : Routes onboarding forms and sends reminders. A new hire completes tax documents, and the system alerts HR and payroll automatically.
- [Predictive analytics](https://www.trinet.com/insights/employee-retention-strategies) : Flags patterns such as attrition risk. AI notices an employee's engagement scores have dropped and prompts the manager to check in.


For the wider technology picture, see our guide to[HR technology trends](https://www.trinet.com/insights/hr-technology-trends) .


##


How are small and midsize businesses using AI in HR now?


AI is a routine part of work at small and midsize businesses, and about half of employers and employees now use it for common HR tasks.


Here's what TriNet's new Annual State of the Workplace report found:


- **Weekly AI use at work reached 75% among employers this year** , up from 66% in 2025 and 53% in 2024. Fifty-one percent of employees use AI at work at least weekly.
- **Across 12 HR tasks, using AI "almost every time or every time" sits between 42% and 54%** , led by writing job descriptions (54% of employers, 51% of employees) and asking benefits questions (50% of both).
- **Employers are open to employees using an AI assistant in the HR platform** , with acceptance running 59% to 67% across eight tasks and highest for training and development (67%).


##


How many people would rather ask AI than a person?


For a general HR question about compensation or benefits, 34% of employees would rather use an AI assistant than an HR administrator, down from 38% in 2025 and 30% in 2024. Employers follow the same curve: 39%, from 45% in 2025 and 40% in 2024.


The more personal the question, the lower the appetite. Twenty-one percent of employees would take a health-related question to AI, and 28% would use AI for a conflict with a colleague.


The takeaway: appetite for an AI-powered HR channel may be leveling off, and most employees still want a person for many scenarios. For the earlier years of this data, see **TriNet's research on**[AI trends in HR](https://www.trinet.com/resources/research/ai-in-hr) .


## ****


Why people choose an AI assistant ****


Speed. A quicker response is the top reason for 46% of employees and 53% of employers who chose AI.


Among employers, "more reliable" fell to 36% and "seems easier" rose to 48%. People pick AI because it's fast, so fast answers plus an easy route to a person are the two design goals for any AI rollout in HR.


##


How to decide which HR tasks to hand to AI


Decide task by task, using what employees and employers each say, and place every HR task in one of three handling levels:


- **AI-first with a human route** : AI answers or completes the task, and a person takes over on request or when a trigger is hit.
- **Human-led with AI support** : A person owns the task and AI drafts, gathers, or schedules.
- **Human only** : A person handles it from start to finish.


##


What employees and employers want AI to support


Both sides hand AI the paperwork first.


**Employees say AI would support these tasks better than an HR administrator:**


- Onboarding: 41%
- Benefits updates and reminders: 39%
- Payroll: 34%
- PTO requests: 32%


**Employers say AI would support these tasks better:**


- Onboarding: 37%
- Offboarding: 36%
- Payroll processing: 35%
- Recruitment: 33%


No task that depends on interpreting people’s behavior or intentions (performance management, office culture, interpersonal issues)


(performance management, office culture, interpersonal issues) clears a third on either side.


One trend worth noting: among employers, training and development rose to 30% from 23%, recruitment rose to 30% from 26%, and benefits administration fell back to 26% from 36%.


##


What employees and employers want people to keep doing.


The two sides prioritize human involvement in different areas.


**Employers emphasizes judgment in:**


- Office culture: 43%
- Interpersonal issues: 35%
- Compensation management: 34%
- Performance management: 34%


**Employees emphasizes human involvement in key moments:**


- Onboarding: 46%
- Offboarding: 42%
- Payroll: 38%


Offboarding employers rank it second for AI at 36%, while 42% of employees want it kept with a person.

**A note on recruitment:** AI can help draft job descriptions and schedule interviews, but people should make hiring decisions, so there needs to be a fast route to a human as well. Some states and cities have rules on automated hiring tools, so it's worth checking state and local requirements or consulting with a professional if you're expanding AI's role in hiring.


##


Why onboarding needs both AI and a person


Onboarding is the task employees most want AI to support (41%) and also the one they most want to be kept with a person (46%). We read this as employees wanting a faster route to a person.


Here's how to split it: AI supports forms, tax documents, equipment requests, scheduling, and first-week questions. A named person, manager or HR contact, owns the welcome, introductions, and check-ins.


New hires want to know their paperwork is moving and they can reach someone who knows their name. AI speeds up the administrative path so the person can focus on making someone feel welcomed and set up for success.


For the full onboarding process, see our guide to[employee onboarding best practices](https://www.trinet.com/insights/employee-onboarding-best-practices) . And for the wider gap between what employers think they provide and what employees experience, see our article on[employee experience strategy](https://www.trinet.com/insights/employee-experience-strategy) .


##


How to pair AI with human HR support for high-stakes moments


For compliance risk, employee relations issues, and separations, employees and employers both trust people more than AI alone.


Here's the share who mostly or completely trust each source in high-stakes HR situations:


- **Internal HR team** : 61% of employees, 75% of employers
- **An external human HR expert** : 57% of employees, 63% of employers
- **Technology or AI support alone** : 46% of employees, 55% of employers


Outright distrust of AI alone reaches 11% of employees and 8% of employers.


Concern about AI in HR eased on every measure in 2026, but employees are now more concerned than employers on every one. Data privacy and lack of empathy sit at the top.


###


Three considerations for high-stakes moments:


1. **Route high-stakes matters to a person by default.** Anything involving health, pay errors, conflict, or separation should go straight to someone with HR expertise.
2. **Use AI to help gather facts and documents for that person.** AI can pull together timelines, policy language, and past conversations, so the HR professional walks into the situation prepared.
3. **Give a small team without deep in-house HR access to outside HR expertise.** Small businesses often don't have a full HR team, so **access to HR experts** becomes part of the system, not a fallback.


The best setup pairs AI for quick answers with HR experts for complex or sensitive issues. Employees get speed when they need it and wisdom when it matters.

##


How to start using AI in HR: Six steps for a small business


Start with routine tasks, build the route to a person, and measure whether people get answers faster. If you're wondering how you should proceed with using AI in HR settings, these six steps give you a practical approach.


###


1. Start with routine, high-volume tasks


Pick one or two tasks from the AI-first tier (benefits reminders, PTO requests, pay stub and payroll questions, onboarding paperwork) and pilot them before expanding.


Here's where HR time goes: employees most often name payroll processing (48%) and benefits management (42%) among the tasks HR spends the most time on. Employers name benefits management (47%) and payroll processing (46%).


Start where the volume is highest and the questions are most repetitive. If your HR team answers the same five benefits questions every week, that's your pilot.


###


2. Build a clear route to a person


Set the triggers that send a question to a person: health matters, pay errors, conflict, anything the employee flags. Pass the conversation along so the employee doesn't have to repeat themselves. And state response times for questions that arrive after hours.


Fifty-nine percent of Gen Z employees agree HR should be a 24/7 function, the highest of any generation. AI can cover routine after-hours questions, such as, "How do I update my address?" or "Where do I find my W-2?" while a person follows up on the rest within the stated time.


The goal isn't to replace people with always-on automation. It's to give employees a faster answer when the question is simple and a clear path to a person when it's not.


###


3. Set privacy rules for employee data


Data privacy is employees' top concern about AI in HR.


Set rules on what data the AI tool can access. Keep health details with a person or a dedicated benefits tool. Use role-based access so managers see only their own team's information. And review how each vendor stores and uses employee data.


Remember that only 21% of employees would take a health question to AI. Most people want a person for anything sensitive, so set up your system with employee preferences in mind.


These steps can help mitigate risk, but no system is foolproof. For a fuller look at AI governance, see our guide to[AI risk and governance for small businesses](https://www.trinet.com/insights/ai-hr-strategy-smb-risk-compliance) .


###


4. Train the HR team and publish AI guidance


The HR team needs to know how to check AI answers and when to override them. And employees need short written guidance on acceptable AI use.


Here's the gap: 90% of employers say they've issued guidance on acceptable AI use, while 66% of employees say they've received any.


Write the guidance in plain language, keep it to one page, if possible, and share it when you roll out the AI tool. For insights on AI policy and how roles are changing, see our article on[AI in the workplace .](https://www.trinet.com/insights/ai-workplace-adoption-smb-leaders)


###


5. Tell employees what AI supports and how to reach a person


Explain at rollout and during onboarding which tasks the AI assistant supports and how to reach a person.


Before you build more, ask employees what they want on demand. Employers think benefits information is what employees most expect on demand (51%), while 36% of employees name it. Employees' top on-demand items are pay stubs (39%) and time and attendance tracking (37%).


Build what people will actually use, not what sounds impressive. For making benefits reminders land, see our guide to[employee benefits communication](https://www.trinet.com/insights/employee-benefits-communication-gap-smb) .


###


6. Measure response time, accuracy, and satisfaction


Speed is why people choose AI, so track it:


- Time to answer
- Share of questions resolved
- Time from hand-off to a person
- Employee satisfaction with both the AI answers and the person who steps in


Review monthly or quarterly and expand to the next task when the numbers hold.


For setting up a simple scorecard, see our guide to **HR metrics** .


###


How to use predictive HR insights once the basics work


Predictive tools are the next step employers want after routine tasks are running.


Every one of the 11 predictive insights tested clears 73% among employers, and identifying employees at risk of leaving leads at 80%. Improving employee engagement is the top intended use at 40%.


Start with attrition risk. When AI flags someone as at risk, treat it as a prompt for a manager conversation, not a decision. Ask what's going on, what support would help, and whether anything about the role or the team needs to change.


Keep decisions with people. AI can spot the pattern. A manager who knows the person can figure out what it means.


For retention tactics, see our guide to[employee retention strategies](https://www.trinet.com/insights/employee-retention-strategies) .


## Methodology note


TriNet's 2027 State of the Workplace report surveyed 525 full-time employers and 575 full-time employees at U.S. companies with 5 to 500 employees, in two surveys fielded in 2026 and administered by Qualtrics.


Small businesses that sort HR tasks deliberately give employees faster answers and give their HR people more time for the moments that need a person. For the full data set, see TriNet's research on AI trends in HR. And if you're ready to explore how AI and HR expertise work together, the TriNet platform and[access to HR experts](https://www.trinet.com/access-hr-experts) can help you support the setup this article describes. The routine work gets faster. The wisdom stays with people. Your team gets both.


## Frequently Asked Questions


Will AI replace HR?


The 2026 data points to AI supporting more routine HR work while people keep the moments that need judgment.


Sixty-one percent of employees and 75% of employers trust an internal HR team for high-stakes situations, compared to 46% and 55% who trust technology or AI support alone. And onboarding—the task employees most want AI to support—is also the one they most want kept with a person.


For a small HR team, this means more time for people-facing work. AI takes the repetitive questions. You take the conversations that shape whether someone stays, grows, or leaves.


What AI tools do HR teams use?


HR teams use four main categories:


- **An AI assistant inside the HR platform** that answers benefits, pay, and PTO questions
- **Generative AI writing tools** for job descriptions, policy summaries, and performance review drafts
- **Recruiting and scheduling tools** that help organize applicant information and coordinate interviews, with human oversight
- **HR analytics** that flag turnover risk and track engagement


Small businesses often get these inside their HR platform rather than buying each one separately, which keeps costs down and data in one place.


Is it safe to use AI with employee data?


It can be, with rules in place.


Set limits on what data the AI tool can access. Review how your vendor stores and uses employee data. Keep a person in charge of sensitive cases like health questions, pay disputes, and conflicts.


Data privacy is employees' top concern about AI in HR, so showing you've thought through the safeguards can help build trust. But no system is without risk, so soft qualifiers matter here: these steps can help mitigate risk, not eliminate it.
